title: Piece values

card.idea: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no number because you can never lose him. Use the numbers to judge whether a trade is a good deal.

explain.text: A rook is worth 5, a knight 3, a bishop 3, a pawn 1. A queen is worth 9, about as much as two rooks. Giving a bishop for a pawn loses two points.
The bishop can take the pawn on f7, but the knight on h6 takes back. You spend 3 to win 1. That is a bad deal even though the capture is legal.

challenges.prompt: Which of these is worth the most?

hints.text: A knight and a bishop are worth the same as each other: three pawns.
hints.text2: The piece on a1 is worth five.

challenges.prompt: Two rooks against a queen: who has more?

hints.text: A rook is worth five and a queen nine.
hints.text2: Two rooks come to ten, which is one more than the queen on d8.

challenges.prompt: The bishop takes the pawn on f7. Is that a good deal?
reasons: The king on a8 takes back.
The knight on h6 takes back and you lose 3 for 1.

hints.text: The king on a8 is nowhere near f7, so it is not the piece that takes back.

challenges.prompt: Two black pieces are free. Take the more valuable one.

wrong.Qxe2: The rook is worth 5. The queen on h4 is worth 9, and it is just as free.

challenges.reason: A queen is worth 9, more than the rook on e2.

wrong.Rxh5: The bishop is worth 3. The rook on g5 is worth 5.

challenges.reason: Rook (5) beats bishop (3) when both are on offer.
The bishop on d4 is worth 3 and nothing takes back.

takeaway: Pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9 — count before you trade.
